messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: new auto-diff + improved existing forward-mode
parts:
I've been putting some cycles into evaluating Michael's new
proposal for auto-diff (I don't think they're written up anywhere ---
he just went over them one afternoon at MCMski with me and Daniel).

The basic idea is that each function stores its first, second, and
third-order derivatives, and then all of the derivatives are calculated
by multiple sweeps back and forth on the expression stack, with no
need for any further virtual function calls.

I'm still worried about the amount of memory this will take for
storing the derivatives for high-dimensional operations like dot products.
The dot product derivatives are quite structured, given that the operation
is just SUM_i x[i] * y[i]. If N is large, we wind up with an N x N
matrix of Hessians, which if you ordered the input vector x[1], y[1],
x[2], y[2], ... should just a narrow off-diagonal band.

We can probably deal with this case by de-vectorizing. That is,
implementing dot(x,y) literally as the sum of individual products.
The downside to this is that it increases the number of items on
the stack for all the intermediate sums and products compared to what
we do now.

The other issue I worry about with the new scheme is that addition
will be less efficient because it's going to require storing the
partials where we often don't need to do that now. This is particularly
worrisome for addition, which doesn't currently require storing the
derivatives (all 1) or multiplying them (1 * x) during derivative
propagation.

On the second topic, I just realized our forward-mode auto-diff
is horrendously inefficient for the uses we have in mind. When
I designed it, I just naively followed existing implementations,
which defined a fwd-mode auto-diff variable as:

template <typename T>
fvar {
T val_;
T d_;
}

(I should've used "tangent_" instead of "d_" to follow conventional
notation.)

BUT, what I now realize is that we can always take the value to
be double. We only ever need the tangent to be an auto-diff variable.
What I should've done was this:

template <typename T>
fvar {
double value_;
T tangent_;
}

The types are all sound because values are only ever computed in
terms of other values, whereas tangent values involve other tangents
and other values, and it's kosher to mix double and anything.

This should lead to *more* than a factor of 2 speedup because of
all the mixed operations currently done on values and tangents.
For example:

template <typename T>
fvar<T> multiply(const fvar<T>& x1,
const fvar<T>& x2) {
return fvar<T>(x1.value_ * x2.value_,
x1.tangent_ * x2.value_ + x1.value_ * x2.tangent_);
}

Here the constructor is just the obvious setter.

Current scheme: 3 multiply(var,var)
1 add(var,var)

New scheme: 1 multiply(double,double)
2 multiply(double,var)
1 add(var,var)

The multiply(double,double) is much faster than multiply(var,var)
and also requires substantially less memory on the stack.
The multiply(double,var) calls require the same amount of memory,
but are faster in that they eliminate a pair of multiplications
during derivative propagation.

This will result in a big savings in both memory and time
compared to the current approach.

And the savings are even more stark at third order, i.e.,
fvar<fvar<var>>, which is now just two doubles and
a var, rather than four var instances!

I actually don't think this will be a very complicated fix to
the code. Of course, testing's going to be a pain for second
order (i.e., fvar<var>) because now the values don't need to
be pulled out of a var, they'll just be doubles.

For evaluation, I'd like to implement the new scheme far enough
that we can compare it to Michael's new scheme. My intuition is
that our current scheme will be more memory efficient and
Michael's new scheme will be faster, even for gradients.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] new auto-diff + improved existing forward-mode
parts:
Without having seen Michael's plans, it's hard to comment much on this.  However, based on Bob's description I have two thoughts:
- Is it really worth this much work to get rid of the virtual function calls?  I've really not seen them popping up in the profiles that much.  A bigger issue is making it easier to implement all the needed derivatives which this would help somewhat however, would it not be better to require each function to provide "dot_grad", "mult_hess" and "apply_3rd" (or something) and then apply those as needed?  This would allow for selective optimization of things like dot_product and sum and allow each function to make the decision of how much needs to be stored.
- I imagine we would want to template out the var type so that, if only first order derivatives are needed, no extra storage or computation is needed using, for instance, the boost::enable_if.

More broadly, I'd be interested in how this would impact functions which take matrices or vectors as parameters.  Right now our ability to implement specialized vari's for handling matrix inverses, log determinants, etc is huge for efficient computation.

Cheers,
Marcus

On 1/19/14, 8:53 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> Without having seen Michael's plans, it's hard to comment much on this.

I'd write it up, but it's pretty complicated and I still only
understand it up to second order. (Though Michael says 3rd order
is just more of the same and he has it working for a few operations.)

> However, based on Bob's description I have two
> thoughts:
> - Is it really worth this much work to get rid of the virtual function calls?
> I've really not seen them popping up in
> the profiles that much.

Absolutely. Check out the Adept paper, which is the
first-order version of what Michael's doing:

http://www.met.reading.ac.uk/clouds/adept/

The real benefit, though, is at higher orders, because
nothing needs to get recalculated other than a string
of multiply-adds. As we're doing things now, we run
the whole log prob function on an fvar<var> for each parameter
to compute a row of the Hessian. But all the partials, which
is where the real work is with all the exps, gamma functions
and what not, get recomputed each time.

> A bigger issue is making it easier to implement all the needed derivatives which this would
> help somewhat however, would it not be better to require each function to provide "dot_grad", "mult_hess" and
> "apply_3rd" (or something) and then apply those as needed? This would allow for selective optimization of things like
> dot_product and sum and allow each function to make the decision of how much needs to be stored.

Yes, we absolutely need to do that so that we can still
run Euclidean HMC quickly. All we need per function is
the local gradient vector, Hessian matrix, and tensor
of 3rd order derivatives.

> - I imagine we would want to template out the var type so that, if only first order derivatives are needed, no extra
> storage or computation is needed using, for instance, the boost::enable_if.
Right.

> More broadly, I'd be interested in how this would impact functions which take matrices or vectors as parameters. Right
> now our ability to implement specialized vari's for handling matrix inverses, log determinants, etc is huge for
> efficient computation.

This is my main concern, too. The problem with having to do
Hessians for something like a dot product is that they're mostly
zeroes. The alternative is unfolding it into a sequence of products
and sums, which defeats the speed of what we have in there now.

And doing something like matrix inverse is even worse as far as this
goes. Without solutions to these problems, I think the new
approach is a non-starter.

Having said all this, I have a scheme to make the existing forward-mode
much faster.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] new auto-diff + improved existing forward-mode
parts:
> So you're proposing to break something like dot product
> apart into a series of multiply-adds? It will take quite
> a bit more memory that way, and I don't see how it'd work
> with something like matrix operations like division (or
> inverse or determinant or whatever).

For the dot product, yes. Dense matrix operations will have dense
derivatives and be different beasts.

Splitting things up should only introduce a few extra ints/bools for indexing
and defining order. To get rid of that we'd need some container class or something
and I'm not sure how to do that without bringing in virtual functions.

> I don't know this for sure, but my guess would be that checking
> for 1 would be as expensive as multiplying by 1. Branching is
> expensive!

Right, hence my hesitance that checking for anything beyond zero
(which saves a ton of operations) will provide any utility.

I'm pretty sure that there's no way to have var-specific optimization
without a static expression graph or virtual functions: the latter is too
slow while the former would require limiting the modeling language
(which I support but would have nontrivial side effects).

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] new auto-diff + improved existing forward-mode
parts:
Let’s be clear — the new approach admits very fast matrix computations
by efficiently computing all of the partials in the instantiation of a node
(leveraging Eigen to its full effect).

The issue here is when we define an operation that has sparse or structure
(but non-zero) higher-order derivatives.  Currently we would not take
advantage of this structure and perform unnecessary loops/operations.
Splitting out the nodes would encode the structure in the expression
graph itself, allowing a compromise between the two approaches.

On Jan 20, 2014, at 1:11 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

More broadly, I'd be interested in how this would impact functions which take matrices or vectors as parameters.  Right
now our ability to implement specialized vari's for handling matrix inverses, log determinants, etc is huge for
efficient computation.

This is my main concern, too.  The problem with having to do
Hessians for something like a dot product is that they're mostly
zeroes.  The alternative is unfolding it into a sequence of products
and sums, which defeats the speed of what we have in there now.

And doing something like matrix inverse is even worse as far as this
goes.  Without solutions to these problems, I think the new
approach is a non-starter.

Having said all this, I have a scheme to make the existing forward-mode
much faster.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] new auto-diff + improved existing forward-mode
parts:
On 1/20/14, 3:13 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Letï¿½s be clear ï¿½ the new approach admits very fast matrix computations

> by efficiently computing all of the partials in the instantiation of a node
> (leveraging Eigen to its full effect).

That's what we do now, with the added overhead of
copying the values of the var into a new matrix.

I don't understand your proposal (both my calc and matrix algebra
fu are weak). If you have an N x N matrix and take an inverse,
what's the Hessian and how do you encode it (if necessary)?

> The issue here is when we define an operation that has sparse or structure
> (but non-zero) higher-order derivatives. Currently we would not take
> advantage of this structure and perform unnecessary loops/operations.

A dot product like

z = SUM_i x[i] * y[i]

has a sparse local Hessian, with only d^2/dx[i]dy[i] = 1 and all other
entries zero.

> Splitting out the nodes would encode the structure in the expression
> graph itself, allowing a compromise between the two approaches.

I think we're talking about the same thing here --- define a bunch of
intermediate x[i] * y[i] nodes, each of which has the same (2 x 2) Hessian
(with 0 diagonal and 1 off diagonal entries).

And then a single node for the sum (only a gradient, no higher-order
derivatives); you could also use N binary sums.

I think I see what the booleans are doing now --- that's for when
the Hessian's all zero? That comparison's not free, but definitely
better than the alternative!

Either way, the new approach will take much more memory than what we do now and
require more multiplies by 1 (we can skip that because the dot-product knows that
the gradient is 1).

Right now, for computing gradients, the dot product of two var N-vectors consumes
a total of 2N+2 pointers + 1 size_t (the 2N for the daughters, one for the mother, and one
for the vtable pointer; size_t is for the size). Plus there's one more pointer on the
actual stack to the memory used. The product of a double and var takes the same amount
of memory, but has fewer propagation ops --- presumably that would be the same in
what you're doing.

With the new scheme I was proposing for reducing
memory in fvar, the Hessian calc won't take much more memory per pass, but
there's the inevitable (2N)^2 entries in the final Hessian. This is assuming
I'm remembering correctly that you need an explicit Hessian for SoftAbs
and not just a Hessian-vector product.

- Bob

Again, we have competing issues here.

Virtual functions or static expression graphs would allow for 
custom calculations at each node, providing a huge speed
up when there’s structure.  The latter is not mutually exclusive
with the new approach.

expression graph, as we have already discussed.

But general matrix ops do not have much structure —

approach verses the old one.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] new auto-diff + improved existing forward-mode
parts:
There are two parts to the Adept auto-diff system.

One's the templating, and yes, that'd make compilation times
even worse. I'm not convinced it's worth the coding hassle
given how many functions we have to deal with.

The other is that it just creates an expression graph consisting
only of nodes and partials, so that the backward pass is just
a bunch of add/multiply ops. Exactly what we're doing for
the probability functions, but without any need for the virtual
function call.

Michael figured out how to extend that scheme to higher-order
derivatives. Actually, Michael just figured it out from
scratch --- only after he explained it did I tell him it
was like what Adept was doing. I'd experimented with the
same scheme a while ago, but couldn't really get it to go
any faster than what we had, but I'm not sure I fully got
rid of the virtual function calls.

The downside of Adept compared to what we're doing now is
that it can be more memory intensive. For instance, in
sums, we only have pointers to the daughter nodes, whereas
the Adept scheme has pointers (really just indexes, and they
use int for that, not actual pointers) and also the partials
for the edges. We are lazy about computing many of the partials,
which saves memory in cases other than just sum. For instance,
an exp node doesn't need to store a partial and a daughter,
just the daughter, because the partial's recoverable as the
value. On the other hand, the Adept-like scheme doesn't
need to store a vtable pointer.

- Bob

parts:
Ok, I see your concern with memory but I'm not sure that's much different than what we're doing now.  We already have to store the value and an adjoint for everything.  For more complex operations we end up storing a bit more than that (e.g., matrix factorizations).  Sure it will get nastier with higher order derivatives, but, to some extent, that's unavoidable.  So long as we can

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] new auto-diff + improved existing forward-mode
parts:
To review:

Forward mode computes scalars, namely,

v^{i} partial_{i} phi
v^{i} w^{j} partial_{i} partial{j} phi
v^{i} w^{j} x^{k} partial_{i} partial_{j} partial_{k} phi

efficiently, and because only one sweep is necessary memory
can be allocated on the stack and grows only as the largest node.

Reverse mode computes vectors, namely

partial_{i} phi
v^{i} partial_{i} partial_{j} phi
v^{i} w^{j} partial_{i} partial_{j} partial_{k} phi,

efficiently, at the expense of having to store everything
on the heap. The savings are significantly, at least an order
of N faster than forward mode.

The new method computes both forward and reverse mode,
but focuses on saving the expression graph so that multiple
sweeps can be made without duplicating any partial evaluations.
It could easily be modified to do forward mode with allocation
only on the stack.

Now the expanded memory footprint for reverse mode goes as
the size of the largest node, which in most cases will be dwarfed
by the size of the full expression graph. Higher-order partials
follow a similar pattern. In particular, the footprint should
grow with some coefficient times the size of the problem,
and if memory is an issue then there are going to be much worse
problems with higher-order methods (RHMC NUTS uses way
more memory than this). In particular, if we template out first-order
and higher-order executables then the memory footprint should be
manageable for really big models.

Now, that said, there are many optimizations that could be made
if we admit polymorphism. Dynamic polymorphism is slow,
static would require a change to the modeling language (loops
are fine, the bounds just have to be constants). Adept very
elegantly used expression templates for static polymorphism
which also allowed the compiler to compile away all kinds of
optimizations.

No, you can _compute_ everything with matrix ops, the results just have to stored in many-to-one nodes.
So an N-to-M function would be stored in the graph as M N-to-1 node, but we can do all of the N-to-M
linear algebra efficiently when we compute all those partials.

Instantiation (i.e. computing the partials) can be specialized right now, it’s just traversal of the graph
that has to be generalized.

On Jan 20, 2014, at 10:00 PM, Marcus Brubaker <marcus.a...@gmail.com> wrote:

then it seems plausible.  I'm still not seeing at all why dot_product would have to be done in terms of scalar ops though...  Also, just to be clear, it's not really dot_product that worries me most, it's things like mdivide_left.  If we have to do dot_product with scalar ops, does that mean we have to do mdivide_left (and hence, Cholesky/QR/etc) with scalar ops?  If so that's really bad but right now I don't see why that has to be the case.
